query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying a mainstream face-centered-cubic high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeNi) with a small addition of silver (~5 at. %) will lower both the steady-state coefficient of friction (CoF) and the specific wear rate by promoting the in-situ segregation of a soft, Ag-rich tribofilm that remains lubricious from room temperature up to ≈700 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Vacuum-arc–melted, homogenized equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (FCC, ≈30–50 µm grains, hardness ≈200 HV).
generation.intervention: Substitutional addition of 5 atomic % Ag to form CoCrFeNi-5Ag high-entropy alloy by the same arc-melting route, followed by identical homogenization heat treatment.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding (pin-on-disk, alumina counter-body, 5 N normal load, 0.1 m s⁻¹ sliding speed, 1000 m sliding distance) conducted in laboratory air over 25 °C–700 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Thermodynamically driven segregation/diffusion of Ag to wear track surfaces and near-surface grain boundaries, forming a continuous Ag-rich (metallic Ag ± thin Ag₂O) tribofilm of nanometre thickness.
generation.mechanism:
1) At low T, the low shear strength of metallic Ag (G ≈ 30 GPa) provides easy interfacial slip, cutting adhesive junctions and lowering CoF.
2) At elevated T, accelerated diffusion maintains Ag supply; mild oxidation produces Ag/Ag₂O glaze with similarly low shear stress, while suppressing abrasive oxide formation from the base HEA.
3) The compliant film redistributes contact stress, delaying third-body abrasion and consequently lowering volumetric wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to undoped CoCrFeNi: (a) steady-state CoF falls from ≈0.80 ± 0.05 to ≤0.30 ± 0.05 at 25 °C and from ≈0.60 ± 0.05 to ≤0.20 ± 0.05 at 700 °C; (b) specific wear rate is reduced by ≥1 order of magnitude (≈10⁻⁴→10⁻⁵ mm³ N⁻¹ m⁻¹) across the full temperature window.
generation.baseline: Identical tribological tests on the Ag-free CoCrFeNi alloy.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness expected for: 2–10 at.% Ag, FCC HEA matrix, temperatures below the Ag melting point (~961 °C) in oxidizing or inert atmospheres. May fail in high vacuum (tribofilm cannot self-replenish) or if sliding speed raises interface above Ag melting point, causing film loss.
generation.uncertainty: No systematic tribological dataset yet exists for Ag-doped CoCrFeNi across the entire 25–700 °C range; possible Ag agglomeration or softening could offset wear improvement, and bulk hardness reduction may become dominant at >800 °C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloys: (1) CoCrFeNi and (2) CoCrFeNi-5Ag by identical melting and homogenization. Conduct dry pin-on-disk tests at 25 °C, 400 °C, 550 °C, and 700 °C under the stated load and speed, recording real-time CoF and collecting post-test wear-track cross-sections.
measurements: Steady-state coefficient of friction (last 100 m segment)
Specific wear rate via wear-track profilometry
Surface chemistry by XPS/AES to confirm Ag-rich film
Cross-section TEM of wear track to measure film thickness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If at ≥3 of the 4 temperatures the Ag-containing alloy fails to show both (i) ≥20 % lower steady-state CoF and (ii) ≥5× lower specific wear rate relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
